title: Foreign Divorce Cannot End a Marriage Solemnised in India, Supreme Court Rules
excerpt: In the N. Sridhar Reddy case, the court held that a UK decree based on irretrievable breakdown fails Section 13 CPC, so the husband's bigamy trial continues — while proceedings against his parents and second wife were quashed.
body:
• The Supreme Court ruled on November 3 that a foreign divorce decree granted on a ground Indian law does not recognise — here, irretrievable breakdown of marriage — cannot automatically dissolve a marriage solemnised in India.
  • Dr N. Sridhar Reddy's bigamy prosecution under Section 494 IPC will continue: he remarried in England 33 days after a Cambridge court made his UK divorce absolute, while his 2003 Hindu marriage in Andhra Pradesh still subsisted in Indian law.
  • The court quashed the case against his parents and his second wife, and held that acquiring foreign citizenship does not shield a spouse from obligations under an Indian marriage.
  • For NRIs: a divorce obtained abroad ends an Indian marriage in India only if the foreign court had jurisdiction recognised under the couple's matrimonial law and granted the decree on a ground that law recognises — otherwise, remarriage can be prosecuted as bigamy in India.

A divorce granted by a foreign court cannot, by itself, end a marriage solemnised in India. Ruling on November 3, a Supreme Court bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar held that a foreign divorce decree obtained on grounds not recognised under Indian personal law offers no immunity against bigamy charges, and that the sanctity of matrimonial status cannot be compromised through forum shopping, according to Legal Republic's report of the judgment in N. Sridhar Reddy v. The State of A.P.

The Case: A UK Divorce, an Indian Marriage

Dr N. Sridhar Reddy married N. Geetha Prasanthi in Andhra Pradesh in 2003 under Hindu rites. A Cambridge County Court in England ordered a decree nisi on November 27, 2013 and made the divorce absolute on January 29, 2014, on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage. Thirty-three days later, on March 3, 2014, Reddy married again in Norfolk, England — even though an Indian court had already refused to dissolve the first marriage. The Andhra Pradesh High Court refused to quash the criminal proceedings against him under Section 494 (bigamy) and Section 120B read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, and he appealed to the Supreme Court.

Why the Decree Failed the Test

The bench framed two questions, the first being whether the foreign decree was entitled to recognition in India under Section 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, which sets the conditions under which a foreign judgment is conclusive. Applying the rule settled in Y. Narasimha Rao v. Y. Venkata Lakshmi (1991), the court held that the jurisdiction the foreign court assumed, and the grounds on which it granted relief, must accord with the matrimonial law under which the parties married. Irretrievable breakdown is not a ground recognised under the Hindu law governing this marriage, so the Cambridge decree fell short.

"Such a decree cannot automatically be accorded recognition in India."

— Supreme Court, N. Sridhar Reddy v. State of A.P., on the UK divorce decree

Because the decree fails Section 13, the first marriage continues to subsist in India, and a subsequent marriage can constitute bigamy regardless of the spouse later acquiring foreign citizenship, Hyderabad Mail reported. The bench also treated bigamy as a continuing offence. While the prosecution against Reddy continues before the trial court in Andhra Pradesh, the same judgment quashed the case against his parents and his second wife.

What This Means for Couples Abroad

The ruling does not bar Indians from divorcing abroad. It restates the conditions under which India will recognise the result: the foreign court's jurisdiction and its grounds must both accord with the law under which the couple married, following Narasimha Rao and the earlier Satya v. Teja Singh line of cases. For the many NRI couples married in India who later separate overseas, the safe course the judgment points to is a divorce on a recognised ground — or proceedings under Indian matrimonial law — before any remarriage. India Today reported the ruling as a clarification that a foreign-country divorce cannot end a marriage in India on its own.
